title: Chapter 41 — Moby Dick
paragraphs: I, Ishmael, was one of that crew. My shouts had gone up with the rest. My oath had been welded with theirs. And I shouted louder and hammered my oath harder because of the dread in my soul. A wild, mystical, sympathetic feeling was in me. Ahab's unquenchable feud seemed like my own. With eager ears I learned the history of that murderous monster against whom I and all the others had sworn our oaths of violence and revenge.

For some time, though only at intervals, the solitary White Whale had haunted those uncivilized seas mostly visited by sperm whale hunters. But not all of them knew of his existence. Only a few had knowingly seen him, and the number who had actually and deliberately fought him was very small. Because of the large number of whale ships, their scattered positions across the entire ocean, with many of them pushing their hunt along lonely latitudes where they might not encounter another vessel for a full year or more, and because of the great length of each voyage and the irregular sailing schedules from home — all of these factors, along with others, had long prevented the news about Moby Dick from spreading through the entire worldwide whaling fleet. It was reasonable to suspect that several ships reported to have encountered, at such and such a time or on such and such a line of longitude, a sperm whale of unusual size and ferocity — which, after doing great damage to its attackers, had completely escaped — that this whale must have been none other than Moby Dick. Yet since the sperm whale fishery had recently seen many instances of great ferocity, cunning, and malice from the whales being hunted, those who had unknowingly fought Moby Dick were mostly content to blame the particular terror he inspired on the general dangers of the sperm whale fishery rather than on this individual creature. That was how most people had understood the disastrous encounter between Ahab and the whale.

As for those who had previously heard of the White Whale and then happened to see him — at first, almost every one of them had lowered for him as boldly and fearlessly as for any other sperm whale. But eventually, such catastrophes resulted from these attacks — not just sprained wrists and ankles, broken limbs, or horrific amputations, but fatalities of the deadliest kind — that these repeated, disastrous defeats, all piling their terrors onto Moby Dick, had gone far toward shaking the courage of many brave hunters who eventually heard the story of the White Whale.

Nor did wild rumors fail to exaggerate and further horrify the true accounts of these deadly encounters. For not only do fantastic rumors naturally grow from the very body of all shocking events, the way a damaged tree sprouts fungi, but in maritime life, far more than on land, wild rumors flourish wherever there is any real foundation for them to cling to. And just as the sea surpasses the land in this respect, so the whale fishery surpasses every other kind of seafaring life in the wonder and terror of the rumors that circulate. For whalemen as a group are no more free from the ignorance and superstition that all sailors inherit than anyone else. But of all sailors, they are by far the most directly exposed to whatever is terrifyingly astonishing in the sea. Face to face they encounter its greatest marvels, and hand to jaw they fight them. Alone, in such remote waters that you could sail a thousand miles past a thousand shores without finding a single welcoming hearth — in such places, doing the work he does, the whaleman is surrounded by influences that make his imagination pregnant with mighty creations.

No wonder, then, that as the rumors of the White Whale gathered force from merely crossing the widest ocean spaces, they eventually absorbed all manner of morbid suggestions and half-formed hints of supernatural forces. In the end, these invested Moby Dick with new terrors borrowed from nothing visible. So much panic did he finally inspire that few who had heard of the White Whale through these rumors alone were willing to face the danger of his jaws.

But there were still other, more practical influences at work. Even today, the original fearsome reputation of the sperm whale, as terrifyingly different from all other whale species, has not died out among whalemen. There are those among them who, though intelligent and brave enough to fight a Greenland or right whale, would perhaps — from inexperience, incompetence, or fear — refuse a battle with the sperm whale. In any case, plenty of whalemen, especially those not sailing under the American flag, have never fought a sperm whale at all. Their knowledge of whales is limited to the less dangerous species hunted in the North. Sitting on their deck hatches, these men listen with childlike wonder and awe to the wild, strange tales of southern whaling. And the supreme terribleness of the great sperm whale is nowhere more deeply understood than aboard the ships that face him.

And as if the now proven reality of his power had, in earlier legendary times, cast its shadow before it, we find some naturalist-authors — Olassen and Povelson — declaring the sperm whale not only to be a terror to every other creature in the sea but so incredibly ferocious as to be perpetually thirsting for human blood. Even as late as Cuvier's time, these or similar impressions persisted. In his Natural History, the Baron himself states that at the sight of the sperm whale, all fish (sharks included) are "struck with the most vivid terror" and "often, in the panic of their flight, dash themselves against rocks so violently as to cause instant death." And however much general fishing experience may correct such reports, in their full terribleness — even down to Povelson's bloodthirsty detail — the superstitious belief in them is, in certain crises, revived in the hunters' minds.

So, overawed by the rumors and omens surrounding him, not a few fishermen recalled, regarding Moby Dick, the earliest days of the sperm whale fishery, when it was often hard to persuade experienced right-whale men to join this new and daring trade. Such men insisted that while other whales might be safely pursued, to chase and lance something as terrifying as the sperm whale was not for mortal man. To attempt it would be to be instantly torn into eternity. On this point, some remarkable documents survive.

Nevertheless, some there were who, even knowing all this, were ready to chase Moby Dick. And an even greater number, having only heard of him vaguely and at a distance, without specific details of any particular disaster and without the supernatural embellishments, were tough enough not to flee from the fight if it came to them.

One of the wild ideas I mentioned, which eventually became linked with the White Whale in superstitious minds, was the eerie notion that Moby Dick was everywhere at once — that he had actually been encountered in opposite latitudes at the very same instant.

Nor, credulous as such people must have been, was this idea entirely without some faint basis in fact. For since the secrets of ocean currents have never been fully revealed, even by the most advanced research, the hidden movements of the sperm whale below the surface remain largely unexplained to his pursuers. From time to time, these mysteries have produced the most curious and contradictory theories, especially about the means by which, after diving to enormous depth, the whale transports himself with such incredible speed to the most distant points.

It is a fact well known to both American and English whale ships, and recorded authoritatively years ago by Scoresby, that some whales captured far north in the Pacific have been found with harpoon barbs in their bodies that were thrown in the Greenland seas. And in some cases, the interval between the two attacks could not have been more than a few days. From this, some whalemen have concluded that the Northwest Passage, so long a puzzle to man, was never a puzzle to the whale. So that here, in the real lived experience of living men, the legendary wonders told in ancient times — about the inland Strello mountain in Portugal, near whose top there was said to be a lake where shipwrecks floated to the surface, and the even more marvelous story of the Arethusa fountain near Syracuse, whose waters were believed to flow underground all the way from the Holy Land — these fabulous tales are nearly equaled by the whalemen's realities.

Forced into familiarity with such wonders, and knowing that after repeated, fearless attacks the White Whale had escaped alive, it can hardly be surprising that some whalemen went further in their superstition. They declared Moby Dick not only everywhere at once but immortal (for immortality is just everywhere-ness in time). Though groves of spears should be planted in his flanks, he would still swim away unharmed. Or if he should ever be made to spout thick blood, that sight would be only a ghostly deception. For again, in unstained waves hundreds of leagues away, his pure white spout would be seen once more.

But even stripped of these supernatural rumors, there was enough in the earthly reality and undeniable character of the monster to strike the imagination with extraordinary power. It was not so much his uncommon size that distinguished him from other sperm whales, but — as mentioned elsewhere — a peculiar snow-white, wrinkled forehead and a high, pyramid-shaped white hump. These were his prominent features, the marks by which, even in the limitless, uncharted seas, he revealed his identity at a great distance to those who knew him.

The rest of his body was so streaked, spotted, and marbled with the same ghostly hue that he had earned his distinctive name of the White Whale. A name literally justified by his vivid appearance when seen gliding at high noon through a dark blue sea, leaving a milky-way wake of creamy foam, all sparkling with golden gleams.

It was not his unusual size, nor his remarkable color, nor even his deformed lower jaw that invested the whale with such natural terror, but rather an unprecedented, intelligent malice that, according to specific accounts, he had displayed over and over in his attacks. Most of all, his treacherous retreats struck more fear than perhaps anything else. For when swimming ahead of his triumphant pursuers, showing every sign of alarm, he had been known several times to turn around suddenly and, bearing down on them, either smash their boats to splinters or drive them back in panic to their ship.

Several deaths had already attended his chase. Though similar disasters, however little publicized on shore, were by no means unusual in the fishery, in most cases the White Whale's actions seemed to show such infernal premeditation that every maiming or death he caused was not regarded as the work of a mindless animal.

Judge, then, to what peaks of inflamed, desperate fury the minds of his more determined hunters were driven when, amid the splinters of shattered boats and the sinking limbs of torn companions, they swam out of the white foam of the whale's terrible rage into the serene, maddening sunlight that smiled on, as if at a birth or a wedding.

His three boats smashed around him, oars and men whirling in the eddies, one captain seized the line-knife from his broken bow and lunged at the whale like an Arkansas duelist at his enemy, blindly trying with a six-inch blade to reach the life buried fathoms deep in the whale. That captain was Ahab. And then it was that Moby Dick, sweeping his sickle-shaped lower jaw beneath him, reaped away Ahab's leg the way a mower cuts a blade of grass. No turbaned Turk, no hired Venetian or Malay assassin could have struck him with more apparent malice. There was little reason to doubt that ever since that nearly fatal encounter, Ahab had nursed a savage hatred for the whale — all the fiercer because in his frenzied state of mind, he eventually came to identify with Moby Dick not just all his physical suffering but all his intellectual and spiritual torments. The White Whale swam before him as the living embodiment of all those malicious forces that some deep-thinking men feel eating away at them until they are left living with half a heart and half a lung. That intangible evil which has existed from the beginning — to whose rule even modern Christians assign half the world, and which the ancient Ophites of the East worshipped in their statue of the devil — Ahab did not bow down before it like them. Instead, deliriously transferring the idea to the hated white whale, he hurled himself, broken as he was, against it. All that most enrages and torments, all that stirs up the dregs of things, all truth laced with malice, all that cracks the sinews and clots the brain, all the subtle demonisms of life and thought — to crazy Ahab, all evil was visibly concentrated and made physically attackable in Moby Dick. He piled upon the whale's white hump the sum of all the rage and hatred felt by his entire race from Adam onward. And then, as if his chest were a cannon, he fired his burning heart's shell upon it.

It is unlikely that this obsession in him sprang up at the precise moment he lost his leg. Then, lunging at the monster, knife in hand, he had only been giving vent to a sudden, passionate, physical fury. And when he received the blow that tore him apart, he probably felt nothing but the agonizing bodily wound. Yet when, forced by this collision to turn homeward, Ahab and his anguish lay stretched together in one hammock for long months of days and weeks, rounding in mid-winter that dreary, howling Patagonian Cape — then it was that his torn body and wounded soul bled into each other, and the mingling drove him mad. That this final obsession seized him only then, on the homeward voyage after the encounter, seems nearly certain from the fact that at intervals during the passage, he was a raving lunatic. Though missing a leg, such vital strength still lurked in his powerful chest, and was intensified by his delirium, that his mates were forced to lash him down even as he sailed, raving in his hammock. In a straitjacket he swung to the mad rocking of the gales. And when, running into calmer latitudes, the ship floated with gentle sails spread across the tranquil tropics, and his madness appeared to have been left behind with the Cape Horn swells, and he came out of his dark den into the blessed light and air — even then, when he showed that firm, composed face, however pale, and gave his calm orders again, and his mates thanked God the terrible madness was gone — even then, deep within his hidden self, Ahab still raved on. Human madness is often a cunning, cat-like thing. When you think it has fled, it may have only transformed itself into some subtler form. Ahab's full lunacy did not subside but contracted and deepened, like the Hudson River, which does not diminish but flows narrowly and unfathomably through the Highland gorge. And just as in his narrowed obsession not one drop of Ahab's broader madness was left behind, so in that broader madness not one drop of his great natural intellect had been destroyed. What had been the living agent now became the living instrument. His particular lunacy had stormed his general sanity and captured it, turning all its concentrated firepower on its own mad target. So far from having lost his strength, Ahab, for that single purpose, now possessed a thousand times more power than he had ever sanely brought to bear on any reasonable goal.

This is much, yet Ahab's larger, darker, deeper part remains only hinted at. But it is useless to try to popularize profundities, and all truth is profound. Winding far down from within the very heart of this spiked fortress where we now stand — however grand and wonderful, now leave it — take your way, you nobler, sadder souls, down to those vast Roman halls beneath, where far below the fantastic towers of man's upper world, his root of grandeur, his whole awful essence sits enthroned in bearded state — an ancient buried beneath antiquities, seated on broken statues! So with a cracked throne, the great gods mock that captive king. So, like a pillar built to support a temple, he sits patiently, holding up on his frozen brow the piled weight of ages. Wind your way down there, you prouder, sadder souls! Question that proud, sad king! There is a family resemblance — yes, he begat you, you young exiled royals. And from your grim father alone will the old state secret come.

Now, in his heart, Ahab had some glimpse of this — namely, that all his means were sane, but his motive and his object mad. Yet without power to kill, change, or escape the fact, he also knew that he had long been deceiving mankind about it — and in some ways still was. But his deception was only subject to his awareness, not to his deliberate will. Nevertheless, he succeeded so well in it that when he stepped ashore on his ivory leg at last, no Nantucketer thought him anything other than naturally grief-stricken, and deeply so, by the terrible accident that had befallen him.

The reports of his undeniable madness at sea were likewise popularly attributed to the same cause. And so too was all the added brooding that had settled on his brow from that day onward, right up to the day he sailed on the Pequod for the present voyage. And it is not so unlikely that, far from doubting his fitness for another whaling voyage because of such dark signs, the calculating people of that practical island were inclined to think that for those very reasons he was all the better qualified and set on edge for a pursuit so full of rage and wildness as the bloody hunt of whales. Gnawed from within and burned from without, with the fixed, unrelenting fangs of some incurable idea — such a man, if he could be found, would seem the very one to drive his iron and raise his lance against the most terrifying of all beasts. Or if for any reason thought to be physically unable, such a man would seem supremely fit to urge and howl his crew onward to the attack. But whatever the truth, this much is certain: with the mad secret of his undiminished rage locked and bolted inside him, Ahab had deliberately sailed on this voyage with one single, all-consuming purpose — hunting the White Whale. Had any of his old acquaintances on shore even half-guessed what was lurking inside him, how quickly their horrified and righteous souls would have torn the ship from such a fiendish man! They had signed on for profitable cruises, the profits counted in dollars from the mint. He was intent on an audacious, implacable, and supernatural revenge.

Here, then, was this gray-headed, ungodly old man, chasing a Biblical whale with curses around the world, at the head of a crew mainly made up of mongrel renegades, castaways, and cannibals — morally weakened, too, by the helplessness of mere unaided virtue in Starbuck, the bulletproof cheerfulness of Stubb, and the pervasive mediocrity of Flask. Such a crew, so officered, seemed specially selected and assembled by some infernal fate to help him in his obsessive revenge. How they responded so completely to the old man's fury — by what dark magic their souls were possessed, so that at times his hatred seemed almost to be theirs, and the White Whale as much their unbearable enemy as his — how all this came to be — what the White Whale meant to them, or how, to their unconscious minds, in some dim, unsuspected way, he might have seemed the gliding great demon of the seas of life — to explain all this would be to dive deeper than Ishmael can go. The underground miner that works in all of us — how can anyone tell where his shaft leads by the ever-shifting, muffled sound of his pick? Who doesn't feel the irresistible arm pulling? What skiff, towed behind a warship, can stand still? For my part, I gave myself up to the madness of the time and place. But while rushing headlong to confront the whale, I could see nothing in that brute but the deadliest evil.
